mainText: Good morning, Landon. Here's your brief for Tuesday, November 17, 2026. First, Wall Street took a hard hit on Monday. The S&P 500 fell almost two percent, the Dow dropped about 740 points, and the Nasdaq lost two and a half percent, pushing it more than ten percent below its October high and into correction territory. Chip stocks led the slide, with a semiconductor index down more than five percent. Next, investors are bracing for a busy stretch in tech. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings today, still dealing with last week's sudden leadership change, and a new federal rule limiting China's access to advanced AI chips is adding pressure. Anthropic's long awaited stock market debut is also expected later this week, and futures markets now see a December interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve as nearly certain. Next, Ukraine launched an overnight drone attack that struck the Kerch Bridge, the road and rail link between Russia and occupied Crimea. Traffic on the bridge was temporarily restricted, with reports of large numbers of vehicles stranded, while Russian air raids on Kyiv caused deaths in the capital. Next, leaders of the United States, Japan, Australia and India are meeting in Manila today for the first Quad summit in two years. President Trump then travels to Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering, where talks with the leaders of China and Russia are planned later this week, with nuclear arms, Iran and Ukraine on the agenda. Next, five European Union countries, Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands, announced plans for a center in Rwanda to hold migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected. The deal is still being negotiated and could begin operating in 2027, while human rights groups have criticized the idea. And finally, a third American aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, joining two others already in the region as tensions with Iran remain high. Diplomatic efforts to end the fighting and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz have so far stalled. Here's your fun fact. In a hallway of the physics department at Oxford University, there is a small bell that has been ringing almost nonstop since 1840, powered by the same pair of batteries the whole time. Scientists estimate it has rung around ten billion times, but they have never opened the batteries to find out exactly what is inside, for fear of ending the experiment. The ringing is so faint that you can barely hear it through its protective glass case. Have a great day.
